faq.q: What is under the glass of a touchscreen?
faq.a: A grid of very thin transparent electrodes, usually made of indium tin oxide, laid in rows and columns. They are invisible, so you see the display straight through them.
asks: Are there wires in a touchscreen?

faq.q: Why does a touchscreen need a finger?
faq.a: Your body conducts electricity and can hold charge. When your finger comes close, it changes the stored charge at the nearby grid crossings. That is why gloves and pencils do not work.
asks: Why don't touchscreens work with gloves?

faq.q: How does the phone know where I touched?
faq.a: A controller chip scans every row and column many times a second and measures the charge at each crossing. The crossings that changed most mark exactly where your finger is.
asks: How does a touchscreen find my finger?

faq.q: How can a touchscreen sense two fingers at once?
faq.a: Each crossing in the grid is measured separately, so the controller can spot several touched places at the same time. That makes pinch-to-zoom possible.
asks: How does pinch to zoom work?

faq.q: Why does a touchscreen go wrong when wet?
faq.a: Water conducts a little and changes the charge on the grid too, so the controller can mistake drops for fingers. Some phones try to tell the difference by the shape of the change.
asks: Why does my screen act strangely in the rain?

facts: Capacitive touchscreens use transparent electrodes, usually made of indium tin oxide.
Ordinary gloves block touch sensing because the fabric does not conduct; touchscreen gloves have conductive threads in the fingertips.
